title: Insert into a Sorted Circular Linked List
description: Brute force to optimized: collecting and re-sorting everything versus a single walk that checks each adjacent pair against three boundary conditions.

sections.title: Insert into a Sorted Circular Linked List

content.title: Insert into a Sorted Circular Linked List

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given a node from a Circular Linked List, sorted in ascending order, insert a new value insertVal so the list remains sorted (and circular). The given node can be ANY single node in the list, not necessarily the smallest. If the original list was empty, create a new single-node circular list. Return the ORIGINAL given node (or the new node, if the list was empty).

blocks.caption: Walking adjacent pairs (prev, curr) finds either the normal in-between spot, or the special max-to-min wrap-around point

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A node from a sorted circular linked list (or null if empty), and a value insertVal to insert"],["Output","The original given node (or a new node, if the list was empty), now part of the correctly sorted circular list including insertVal"],["Goal","Correctly handle the normal case, the wrap-around boundary case, and the all-equal-values edge case"],["Constraints","0 <= number of nodes <= 5*10^4; -10^6 <= Node.val, insertVal <= 10^6"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The list is CIRCULAR, so there is no fixed \"smallest\" starting point given","Walking adjacent pairs (prev, curr) around the WHOLE circle, watching for either a normal fit or the special wrap-around point"],["Multiple special cases: new minimum, new maximum, all values equal","A specific set of boundary conditions must be checked explicitly, in addition to the straightforward \"fits between two values\" case"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Since the list is circular and the given starting node could be ANYWHERE in it (not necessarily the smallest value), finding the correct insertion point requires walking all the way around if necessary, watching specifically for the point where the list "wraps" from its largest value back to its smallest.

blocks.title: Analogy: Inserting a New Time Slot Into a Repeating Daily Schedule
blocks.text: Imagine a repeating daily schedule (like clock positions around a circular clock face), and you are handed a reference to just ONE entry in it, not necessarily the earliest. To insert a new time slot correctly, you would walk around the schedule looking for two adjacent entries where the new time fits directly between them, OR, watch for the one special point where the schedule "wraps around" from the latest time of day back to the earliest, which is also a valid place to insert a new earliest-or-latest time.

blocks.caption: The point where prev.val > curr.val is the unique max-to-min wrap-around boundary; a new overall min or max value belongs there

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: circular list 3->4->1->(back to 3), given node value 3, insertVal = 2

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Walk pairs: (3,4) no fit, (4,1) is the wrap-around point (4 > 1); does 2 >= 4 or 2 <= 1? No","Not the wrap point for 2","Neither condition holds, so 2 does not belong here"],["Continue: (1,3) is now checked; is 1 <= 2 <= 3? Yes","Insert between 1 and 3","A normal in-between fit"],["Answer","3->4->1->2->(back to 3)","The value 2 correctly slots in between 1 and 3"]]}

blocks.text: Example: circular list [1] (single node), insertVal = 0

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Only pair available: (1,1) (the single node connects to itself)","prev.val (1) > curr.val (1) is false; not a normal fit either; loop completes (prev returns to head)","Since there is only one node, no other comparison is possible"],["Insert anywhere (the loop's fallback)","1->0->(back to 1)","With only one existing node, any insertion point produces a valid sorted circular list"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before naively re-sorting the entire list from scratch, notice that walking ADJACENT PAIRS around the circle, watching specifically for the max-to-min wrap-around point, correctly handles every case (normal fit, new overall max/min, and all-equal values) in a single pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In the NORMAL case, insertVal simply needs to fit between some adjacent pair (prev, curr) where prev.val <= insertVal <= curr.val.

Observation 2: Because the list is circular, there is exactly ONE point where prev.val > curr.val (the transition from the largest value back to the smallest); this is the ONLY place a new overall maximum or minimum value can correctly be inserted.

Observation 3: If insertVal is either >= the current maximum (prev.val at that wrap point) OR <= the current minimum (curr.val at that wrap point), it belongs exactly at this wrap-around boundary.

Observation 4: If a full loop completes without ever finding either condition, EVERY value in the list must be equal (or there is only one node), so inserting at the ORIGINAL starting position is a valid fallback.

Recognizing that these three checks together (normal fit, wrap-around boundary, full-loop fallback) cover every possible case is what makes this problem's many edge cases tractable.

This is a single walk around the circular list, checking each adjacent pair for either a normal in-between fit or the special max-to-min wrap-around point, with a full-loop fallback for the all-equal-values case.
6. Brute Force Solution
Collect every value from the circular list, add the new value, and sort everything together, ignoring that the list was already sorted (aside from the wrap-around point).
Step by step algorithm

items: Walk the circular list once (starting from the given node, until returning to it), collecting all values.
Add insertVal to the collected values and sort the combined list.

codes.python:
def insert(values, insert_val):                                             # values already given starting from SOME node, in circular order
    if not values:
        return [insert_val]
    combined = sorted(values + [insert_val])                               # simplest correct approach: just re-sort everything together
    return combined


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(insert([3, 4, 1], 2))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Sorting from scratch ignores the fact that the existing list was already sorted (except at one wrap point), doing unnecessary extra work.
This approach does not actually preserve the ORIGINAL given node reference as the returned head, which the real problem specifically requires.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly produces the right final sorted VALUES, since a full sort always produces correct order regardless of the input's prior structure.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), for the sort.
Space: O(n), for the collected array.

Limitation: re-sorting from scratch is unnecessary extra work given the list was ALREADY sorted; walking adjacent pairs once achieves the correct insertion directly in O(n) time, while also correctly preserving the original given node reference.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force ignores the list's existing sorted structure. Instead, walk adjacent pairs (prev, curr) starting from the given node: if insertVal fits normally between them (prev.val <= insertVal <= curr.val), insert there. If (prev, curr) straddles the wrap-around point (prev.val > curr.val) and insertVal is a new overall max or min, insert there instead. If a full loop completes without either condition triggering, insert right after the original starting node (the safe fallback for the all-equal-values case).

Handle the empty-list case directly (a new self-pointing node). Otherwise, walk prev = head, curr = head.next, checking each pair against the three conditions (normal fit, wrap-around fit, full-loop-completed) until one triggers, then insert the new node between prev and curr.
9. Optimized Solution
Walk adjacent pairs around the circular list once, inserting at the first pair satisfying either the normal fit or the wrap-around boundary condition.
Dry run for circular list 3->4->1->(back to 3), insertVal = 2

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pair checked","prev.val <= 2 <= curr.val?","Wrap-around (prev>curr) and 2>=prev or 2<=curr?","Result"],"rows":[["(3,4)","3<=2? No","Not a wrap point (3<4)","Continue"],["(4,1)","4<=2? No","Wrap point (4>1); 2>=4? No. 2<=1? No","Continue"],["(1,3)","1<=2<=3? Yes","-","Insert here"]]}

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The value 2 is inserted between 1 and 3, giving the circular list 3->4->1->2->(back to 3), matching the expected result.

codes.python:
def insert(head, insert_val):
    new_node = ListNode(insert_val)
    if not head:
        new_node.next = new_node                                            # a brand new circular list of size 1
        return new_node

    prev, curr = head, head.next
    while True:
        if prev.val <= insert_val <= curr.val:                              # normal case: insertVal fits directly between prev and curr
            break
        if prev.val > curr.val:                                             # prev/curr straddles the max->min wrap-around point
            if insert_val >= prev.val or insert_val <= curr.val:            # insertVal is a new max OR a new min
                break
        prev, curr = curr, curr.next
        if prev == head:                                                    # completed a full loop: all values must be equal, insert anywhere
            break

    prev.next = new_node
    new_node.next = curr
    return head


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n1 = ListNode(1)
    n3 = ListNode(3)
    n4 = ListNode(4)
    n3.next = n4
    n4.next = n1
    n1.next = n3
    result = insert(n3, 2)
    values = []
    node = result
    for _ in range(4):
        values.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single walk around the circular list, at most once.
Space: O(1) extra, only a couple of pointers used.
Why This Works

The three conditions checked together are exhaustive: either insertVal fits normally somewhere in the middle of the sorted sequence, or it needs to become the new overall maximum or minimum (which can ONLY correctly happen at the unique wrap-around point), or every value in the list is identical (handled by the full-loop fallback, where inserting anywhere is equally valid).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["insertVal fits between some normal adjacent pair","Inserted directly there"],["insertVal is a new overall maximum or minimum","Inserted at the unique wrap-around point (where prev.val > curr.val)"],["Every value in the list is equal (or the loop completes without finding either condition)","Inserted right after the original starting position, a safe fallback"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The empty-list case is handled completely separately upfront, since there is no existing structure to walk at all.
The loop's termination condition (prev returning to head) guards against an infinite loop in the all-equal-values case, where neither the normal-fit nor wrap-around condition would ever trigger.
Checking the wrap-around condition as "insertVal >= prev.val OR insertVal <= curr.val" (not AND) correctly captures BOTH becoming a new maximum and becoming a new minimum in one combined check.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (collect all, re-sort from scratch)","O(n log n)","O(n)","Ignores the list's existing sorted structure; does not preserve the original node reference"],["Optimized (single walk, three boundary conditions)","O(n)","O(1) extra","Directly exploits the existing sorted (circular) structure"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Inserting into a sorted CIRCULAR list requires explicitly handling the unique wrap-around point (where the largest value connects back to the smallest) as a special case, in addition to the normal "fits between two values" check, plus a fallback for when every value happens to be equal.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting the wrap-around special case entirely, which would fail to correctly insert a new overall maximum or minimum value.
Using AND instead of OR when checking the wrap-around condition, which would incorrectly require insertVal to be BOTH a new max AND a new min simultaneously (impossible except in trivial cases).
Missing the full-loop termination check, causing an infinite loop when every value in the list is identical.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Empty list (given node is null)","A brand new node is created, pointing to itself, forming a circular list of size 1"],["Single-node list","The full-loop fallback correctly handles insertion, since there is no other node to compare against"],["insertVal is smaller than every existing value, or larger than every existing value","Correctly inserted at the unique wrap-around point"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly enumerating all THREE cases (normal fit, wrap-around boundary, all-equal fallback) up front, before writing any code, helps avoid missing one of the trickier edge cases mid-implementation.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Insert into a SORTED CIRCULAR linked list" points toward walking adjacent pairs while specifically watching for the unique max-to-min wrap-around point, plus a full-loop fallback for the all-equal-values case.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why is there guaranteed to be AT MOST one wrap-around point (where prev.val > curr.val)? Because the list is sorted in a single ascending pass before wrapping back to the start; a sorted circular sequence has exactly one such "drop" point (or none, if all values are equal).

How would you modify this to insert into a DOUBLY linked circular list? The same three conditions apply identically; an additional prev-pointer update would be needed alongside the existing next-pointer updates.

What if the list could contain duplicate values equal to insertVal? The algorithm still works correctly, since the normal-fit condition uses non-strict inequalities (<=), correctly allowing insertion adjacent to equal values.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A specialized circular-list variant of the general "insert into a sorted linked list" technique, requiring the additional wrap-around boundary check that a non-circular sorted list would never need.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (single walk, three boundary conditions): O(n) time, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Single walk around a sorted circular list, checking adjacent pairs against three boundary conditions
Core Idea: Insert at a normal in-between fit, OR at the unique max-to-min wrap-around point (for a new overall max/min), OR anywhere as a fallback if every value is equal
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: A sorted circular list has at most ONE point where prev.val > curr.val, and that point is exactly where a new overall maximum or minimum must be inserted
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Normal fit, OR the max->min wrap point, OR (full loop) insert anywhere
